Family Health

Sinus infection or COVID-19? Symptoms, testing and what to do next

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A blocked nose, headache and tiredness do not always reveal which illness you have. Sinus inflammation and COVID-19 can overlap, and sometimes occur together. The useful next step depends on your symptoms, risk factors, test results and how the illness is changing.

Sinusitis and COVID-19 describe different things

The sinuses are air-filled spaces around the nose, cheeks and forehead. When their lining becomes inflamed, swelling can interfere with mucus drainage and cause pressure or congestion. This is sinusitis. Viruses cause many episodes, although bacteria can sometimes be involved.

COVID-19 is the illness caused by SARS-CoV-2. It can affect the upper airways and other parts of the body. A person with COVID-19 can have nasal and sinus symptoms, and another condition can occur at the same time. The labels are not mutually exclusive, and a symptom comparison cannot replace testing or an assessment when needed.

The symptoms overlap considerably

A runny or blocked nose, headache, sore throat, cough, fever and tiredness can occur in respiratory illnesses, including COVID-19 and an illness associated with sinus inflammation. The absence of fever does not reliably exclude infection. How unwell you feel, your exposure history and the course over several days all matter.

Avoid deciding that a familiar-feeling cold must be the same illness you had before. Different infections can feel alike, and repeat COVID-19 infections do not always produce the same symptoms. Until the cause is clearer, take sensible precautions around others, particularly anyone at higher risk of severe illness.

Facial pressure can suggest sinus involvement

Sinus symptoms may include tenderness around the cheeks, forehead or eyes, pressure when bending forward, mucus dripping down the throat, toothache, bad breath and a reduced sense of smell. Nasal mucus may become thicker or look yellow or green.

These features help describe the problem but do not identify the germ. Coloured mucus alone does not prove a bacterial infection or establish that an antibiotic is needed. Severe one-sided pain, worsening illness or eye symptoms deserve assessment rather than a home diagnosis based on the colour of a tissue.

Body symptoms and smell changes are not exclusive tests

COVID-19 may also cause body aches, breathlessness, nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. A new loss or change of smell or taste can be a clue, but its frequency varies with the circulating virus and the person’s circumstances. Nasal inflammation and other infections can affect smell too.

There is no dependable symptom checklist that makes these conditions completely separate. Nor is there a fixed day on which everyone’s smell returns. If the change persists, ask for advice. Meanwhile, take extra care with smoke or gas alarms and food safety if you cannot rely on your nose.

Onset and season provide context, not certainty

COVID-19 symptoms can appear in the days after an exposure; public-health guidance describes a possible range of 2–14 days, although timing varies. Some illnesses begin abruptly and others gradually. That difference is not reliable enough to decide whether testing is needed.

Sinus inflammation often follows a cold. Allergies to pollen or animal dander, exposure to smoke and other nasal problems can also contribute to congestion or poor drainage. An allergen is not itself an infectious germ. Colds and some respiratory viruses have seasonal peaks, but COVID-19 can circulate throughout the year. Do not use the calendar to rule it out.

Recovery times vary more than a simple comparison suggests

Acute sinus symptoms commonly improve over a few weeks. Many mild COVID-19 illnesses also improve at home, but a cough, tiredness or other symptoms may last longer than the initial fever. Improvement should be considered alongside your ability to drink, breathe comfortably and manage ordinary activities.

A historical US outpatient study from 2020 illustrates the variation. Among 270 people with information about return to usual health, 175 reported recovery, with a median of seven days from testing among that recovered group. The other 95 had not returned to usual health at the interview, conducted roughly two to three weeks after testing. It did not show that everyone recovered in a week, and those early-pandemic findings cannot predict an individual’s recovery now.

Test when COVID-19 is possible

Testing can help you decide about treatment and precautions. A single negative home antigen test does not rule out infection. For someone with symptoms, current US guidance recommends repeating an antigen test after 48 hours, for at least two tests in total. A clinician may recommend a molecular test or a different local pathway.

Follow the instructions for your particular test and tell the clinician when symptoms started. If you are at increased risk of becoming seriously ill, contact care promptly rather than waiting through several days of testing. Treatment assessment may be appropriate before a positive result is available.

Ask early about treatment if your risk is higher

Age, immune suppression and some long-term conditions can increase the risk of severe COVID-19. Pregnancy and recent pregnancy also matter. Contact your maternity or healthcare team early if you are pregnant or recently gave birth and develop symptoms, even if they seem mild at first.

Antiviral treatment for eligible people needs to begin quickly, generally within five to seven days depending on the medicine. Examples include nirmatrelvir with ritonavir and intravenous remdesivir. A clinician checks timing, interactions, kidney or liver considerations and pregnancy suitability. Appropriate treatment should not be withheld solely because someone is pregnant or breastfeeding, but that does not make every antiviral suitable for every pregnancy.

Home comfort measures should be simple and safe

Rest, drink enough to avoid dehydration and use comfortable food and fluids as tolerated. A warm compress over the face may ease pressure. Saline spray may help nasal discomfort. If you use a sinus-rinsing device, use distilled or sterile water, or water that has been properly boiled and cooled, and follow cleaning instructions. Ordinary unboiled tap water is not suitable for nasal rinsing.

Avoid leaning over a bowl of hot water for steam inhalation. Spills can cause serious scalds, especially around children, and there is no strong evidence that this speeds recovery. A comfortable shower may feel soothing, but it is not an antiviral treatment. Ask a pharmacist about pain or fever relief, avoid duplicate ingredients in combination products and check suitability in pregnancy or for a child. Do not share adult cold medicines with children.

Antibiotics are not automatically needed for sinus symptoms

Most sinus infections do not benefit from antibiotics because a virus is often responsible and the illness may settle on its own. A clinician may suggest observation or a delayed prescription in an appropriate case. Antibiotics do not treat COVID-19 itself, although a separate bacterial infection may sometimes need treatment.

Arrange a review for symptoms lasting more than ten days without improvement, worsening after an initial improvement, fever lasting longer than three or four days, or substantial facial pain. Repeated episodes also deserve discussion. The decision about antibiotics depends on the whole assessment rather than a single symptom or a fixed promise that every sinus illness is harmless.

Hospital treatment depends on the severity of illness

Someone with severe COVID-19 may need oxygen and treatment for complications. Remdesivir is used in selected settings; a steroid such as dexamethasone may be used when COVID-19 causes an oxygen requirement. Steroids are not a routine home remedy for mild COVID-19 without low oxygen. Very severe illness can require intensive care and breathing support, including a ventilator.

Older treatment lists also mention anti-SARS-CoV-2 monoclonal antibodies. Their role depends on the product, current variants and local authorization; some earlier treatments lost usefulness as the virus changed. Preventive antibodies offered to selected immunocompromised people are not interchangeable with treatment for an active infection. High-titer convalescent plasma has a specialist role for some immunocompromised patients, rather than being routine treatment for everyone with COVID-19.

Recognise symptoms that need emergency assessment

Get emergency help for difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain or pressure, new confusion, inability to wake or stay awake, or unusually pale, grey or blue lips, skin or nail beds. The appearance can vary with skin tone. Tell the dispatcher or receiving service that COVID-19 is possible, but do not delay urgent care while trying to confirm a test.

Sinus symptoms also need urgent assessment if accompanied by swelling or redness around an eye, double or reduced vision, difficulty moving the eye, severe frontal headache, swelling over the forehead, a stiff neck or new neurological symptoms. These are different from ordinary mild congestion. Seek care whenever the illness is severe or rapidly worsening, even if it does not fit a checklist.

Reduce the chance of spreading a respiratory infection

While unwell, stay away from others as much as practical, improve ventilation and consider a well-fitting mask when sharing space. A separate sleeping area or bathroom can help if available. Keep hands clean, cover coughs and clean commonly touched surfaces. Let close contacts know if they may have been exposed, so they can follow local advice and protect vulnerable people.

Follow the guidance where you live. As an example, current US community guidance allows a return to normal activities once symptoms have been improving overall and fever has been absent without fever-reducing medicine for at least 24 hours. It then advises five days of added precautions. If fever returns or you worsen, stay home again. Healthcare settings and some workplaces have different rules, and feeling better does not instantly mean you cannot transmit infection.

Persistent symptoms deserve support

Some people have continuing or recurring fatigue, breathlessness, difficulty concentrating or remembering, palpitations, muscle pain or joint pain after COVID-19. These symptoms can affect work, childcare and everyday life. They should not be dismissed simply because the initial infection seemed mild.

Discuss persistent symptoms with a clinician and explain how they affect daily activities. Assessment can consider Long COVID as well as other causes that need treatment. You do not need to wait until a formal duration threshold is reached to ask for help. New chest pain, severe breathlessness or other emergency signs require urgent care rather than a routine follow-up.

Recovery does not remove the need for future prevention

A previous infection does not guarantee lasting protection from another infection. Vaccination decisions should follow current recommendations for your age, health and country. If you have recently recovered, discuss the timing of the next eligible dose with your clinician; a short delay may sometimes be considered according to risk and local guidance.

Tell the team if you received antibody treatment or convalescent plasma, but do not assume that an old universal ninety-day vaccine delay still applies. Recommendations have changed since the early pandemic. Keep the dates of symptoms, tests and treatments available, so that future advice is based on your actual course rather than an outdated general rule.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Symptoms, mucus colour and season alone cannot reliably distinguish COVID-19 from other causes of sinus symptoms.

Testing and early treatment assessment matter for people at higher risk. Local public-health and prescribing guidance can change.

How BeMama can help

Record when symptoms started, test results, current medicines and pregnancy or other risk factors before contacting care.

When to seek help

Breathing difficulty, persistent chest pressure, confusion or inability to stay awake needs emergency care. Eye swelling, vision changes or severe neurological symptoms with sinus pain also need urgent assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Sinusitis describes inflammation; COVID-19 identifies a particular infection.
  • A negative antigen test may need repeating, and higher-risk people should seek advice early.
  • Avoid hot-water steam bowls and use safe water for nasal rinsing.
  • Follow current local precautions rather than an old fixed isolation rule.

Frequently asked questions

Does green mucus prove that I need antibiotics?

No. Mucus colour alone does not establish bacterial infection. Duration, severity and examination help guide treatment.

Can COVID-19 cause sinus-like symptoms?

Yes. Nasal congestion and related symptoms overlap, and another sinus condition can coexist.

Is loss of smell unique to COVID-19?

No. It can occur with nasal inflammation and other infections, and not everyone with COVID-19 loses smell.

What if my first home COVID-19 test is negative?

A single antigen test can miss infection. With symptoms, current US guidance advises a repeat after 48 hours; follow local and test-specific instructions.

Should pregnancy make me wait before seeking treatment?

No. Seek early advice. A clinician can select appropriate treatment and should not withhold it solely because of pregnancy or breastfeeding.

Did the 2020 study show that everyone recovered in seven days?

No. Seven days was the median from testing among those reporting recovery; 35 percent had not returned to usual health when interviewed.

Is steam over a bowl of hot water a good remedy?

No. It can cause serious scalds and has no strong evidence of speeding recovery. Use safer comfort measures.

Can I rinse my nose with ordinary tap water?

Use distilled, sterile or properly boiled and cooled water. Follow the device’s cleaning instructions.

Do I always need to isolate for ten days?

Follow current local rules. Community, healthcare and individual circumstances can differ; old blanket ten-day advice is not a universal current rule.

When do sinus or COVID-19 symptoms need emergency help?

Breathing difficulty, persistent chest pressure, confusion or inability to stay awake need emergency care. Eye swelling or vision change, severe frontal headache and neurological signs with sinus symptoms also need urgent assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
